name: Cotton ball diet
lead: The cotton ball diet is a fad diet in which people swallow cotton balls, sometimes dipped in juice, lemonade or smoothies, in place of food. The goal is a slimmer body: the balls are meant to fill the stomach and suppress hunger so that calorie intake falls and weight comes off, which practitioners hope will give a leaner, thinner look.[1][2]

The practice circulated on forums, chat rooms and video sites around 2013. Accounts describe a June 2013 interview in which model Bria Murphy said some models eat cotton balls soaked in juice to stay thin, and news outlets covered the diet in November 2013.[1][2] Wikipedia cites coverage by ABC News, CBS Atlanta and Guardian Express from late November 2013.[1]

Health professionals quoted in that coverage warn that cotton cannot be digested and can form a blockage, and Wikipedia reports that medical commentators regard the practice as a sign of an eating disorder.[1][2][3] It has no formal scientific or commercial backing.[2]

paras: Practitioners ingest cotton balls, often soaked in juice, lemonade or smoothies, in place of meals; the intended effect is a sense of fullness from a non-caloric filler.[1][2] Wikipedia notes that the cotton cannot be broken down and so is swallowed whole.[1]

The diet spread through online forums and video sites around 2013, with a June 2013 remark by model Bria Murphy about models using the method cited as bringing it attention in fashion.[2] Late-November 2013 stories from ABC News, CBS Atlanta and Guardian Express carried it into mainstream coverage, and Wikipedia places it among 2010s fads and trends.[1] It has no formal scientific or commercial backing.[2]

Wikipedia reports that health commentators warn the cotton can block the digestive tract, with dehydration and bowel obstruction that can harm the intestines and other organs, and that swallowing it whole poses a choking risk.[1] The same source says most so-called cotton balls are bleached polyester, raising concern about chemicals, and that medical commentators view the practice as a sign of an eating disorder.[1]

A 2024 preprint describes bezoars, packed masses of undigested material that can cause gastrointestinal obstruction, as a serious consequence of eating cotton balls to fill the stomach.[3] People worried about disordered eating can find support through national eating disorder helplines.
No studies found. A 2024 preprint discusses bezoar formation from eating cotton balls to fill the stomach.[3]

timeline.event: Model Bria Murphy remarks on the practice in a June interview; news outlets including ABC News and CBS Atlanta cover the diet in November.[1][2]

card.summary: Swallowing cotton balls to feel full; condemned by health experts for blockage risk.
card.note: Documented risk of intestinal blockage requiring surgery.

quick.overview:
The cotton ball diet involves swallowing cotton balls, often dipped in juice, in place of food to feel full.

It was reported as an online fad around 2013 and has been condemned by health professionals.
quick.mechanism: The balls are meant to fill the stomach with a non-caloric bulk. Cotton is not digestible.
quick.risks: Reported risks include bezoars and intestinal obstruction needing surgery, malnutrition, choking, and concern that it signals disordered eating.

chain: Cotton balls swallowed in place of food
Stomach feels full with no calories
Lower intake aimed at a thinner body
angle.text: Followers use cotton balls as a no-calorie filler to cut food intake and lose weight quickly. Health professionals quoted in news coverage describe documented risks of the method.
